claim: On 2025-06-17 AWS extended mandatory root user MFA to member accounts, so the root user of every account type must use MFA; the requirement began with management account root users in May 2024 and standalone account root users in June 2024.
question: When did root user MFA become mandatory for every AWS account type, and in which order did it roll out?

evidence.quote: Today AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) announced comprehensive multi-factor authentication (MFA) requirements for root users across all account types, with the expansion to member accounts.

Our security journey began with requiring MFA for AWS Organizations management account root users in May 2024, followed by expanding MFA requirements to standalone account root users in June 2024, and introducing centralized root access management for AWS Organizations in November 2024.
All AWS account types (standalone, management, and member accounts) require MFA to be configured for their root user.

changed.was: requiring MFA for AWS Organizations management account root users in May 2024

note: d094. Older questions treat root MFA as a recommended best practice; 'enable MFA on the root user' stays the right answer. Current truth: iam-root-mfa-required-all-account-types.

claim: AWS Organizations added full IAM policy language support for SCPs: Allow statements in an SCP can now use conditions, individual resource ARNs and the NotAction element, and SCPs can use the NotResource element and wildcards at the beginning or middle of Action strings.
question: Which policy elements can SCP Allow statements use since the full IAM policy language launch?

values.display: conditions, individual resource ARNs, and the NotAction element with Allow statements
values.spoken: conditions, resource ARNs and NotAction in Allow statements

evidence.quote: With this launch, SCPs now support use of conditions, individual resource ARNs, and the NotAction element with Allow statements. Additionally, you can now use wildcards at the beginning or middle of Action element strings and the NotResource element.
| [Condition](#scp-syntax-condition) | Specifies conditions for when the statement is in effect. | `Allow,``Deny` |
| [Resource](#scp-syntax-resource) | Specifies the AWS resources that the SCP applies to. | `Allow,``Deny` |

note: d100. What's New posted 2025-09-19 (change feed). No page states the old rule verbatim, so `changed` is empty. Older material says SCP Allow statements cannot use Condition or Resource; that is outdated. The SCP stays a permission ceiling that never grants.

claim: On 2024-11-13 AWS Organizations added resource control policies (RCPs), which set the maximum permissions for resources in the accounts of an organization or OU; an explicit deny in an RCP overrides an allow, like an explicit deny in an SCP.
question: When were RCPs introduced and what do they limit?

evidence.quote: | [Support for AWS Organizations resource control policies (RCPs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/access_policies.html#access_policy-types) | Use an AWS Organizations resource control policy (RCP) to define the maximum permissions for resources within accounts in your organization or organizational unit (OU). RCPs limit permissions that identity-based and resource-based policies can grant to resources in accounts within your organization. | November 13, 2024 |

| [Added resource control policies (RCPs)](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/organizations/latest/userguide/orgs_manage_policies_rcps.html) | You can use resource control policies (RCPs) to control the maximum available permissions for resources in an organization. | November 13, 2024 |
An explicit deny in the identity-based policy, an SCP, or an RCP overrides the allow.

note: d100. Before November 2024 only SCPs existed as organization authorization policies; older questions never mention RCPs. RCPs cover a subset of services (iam-rcp-subset-of-services).

claim: On 2024-11-14 IAM added centralized root access for member accounts of AWS Organizations: the root user credentials of member accounts can be removed centrally, and privileged root tasks run through short-term sessions from the management account or a delegated administrator for IAM.
question: Since when can an organization remove member-account root credentials centrally, and how are root-only tasks done afterwards?

evidence.quote: | [Centrally manage root access for member accounts](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_root-user.html#id_root-user-access-management) | You can now manage privileged root user credentials across member accounts in AWS Organizations with centralized root access. Centrally secure the root user credentials of your AWS accounts managed using AWS Organizations to remove and prevent root user credential recovery and access at scale.+   [Root user best practices](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/root-user-best-practices.html)   | November 14, 2024 |

The AWS Organizations management account or a delegated administrator account for IAM can perform some privileged tasks on member accounts that would otherwise require root user credentials. With centralized root access, these tasks are performed through short-term privileged sessions.

note: d101. New best answer to 'remove or prevent root credentials across all member accounts'. Older answers: SCP that denies root actions in member accounts (still valid as a preventive control).

claim: After root access is centralized, you can delete root user credentials (password, access keys, signing certificates, MFA) from member accounts; new accounts created in AWS Organizations then have no root user credentials by default, and member accounts cannot sign in as root or recover the root password.
question: What happens to member-account root credentials after you centralize root access?

values.display: delete root user credentials from member accounts
values.spoken: delete root user credentials from member accounts

values.display: no root user credentials by default
values.spoken: no root user credentials by default

qualifiers.scope: per member account of an organization

evidence.quote: After you centralize root access, you can choose to delete root user credentials from member accounts in your organization. You can remove the root user password, access keys, signing certificates, and deactivate multi-factor authentication (MFA). New accounts you create in AWS Organizations have no root user credentials by default. Member accounts can't sign in to their root user or perform password recovery for their root user.

note: d101 current truth. To recover a member root password later, a privileged task with 'Allow password recovery' is needed.

claim: Since 2022-11-16 the root user and each IAM user can register up to eight MFA devices of any type (FIDO security keys, virtual authenticator apps or hardware TOTP tokens), and one device is enough to sign in.
question: Since when can one user register several MFA devices, and how many?

qualifiers.scope: per root user or IAM user

evidence.quote: | [Support for multiple multi-factor authentication (MFA) devices for root users and IAM users](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/id_credentials_mfa.html) | Now you can to add up to eight MFA devices per user, including FIDO security keys, software time-based one-time password (TOTP) with virtual authenticator applications, or hardware TOTP tokens. | November 16, 2022 |

Your AWS account root user and IAM users can register up to eight MFA devices of any type. Registering multiple MFA devices can provide flexibility and help you reduce the risk of access interruption if a device is lost or broken. You only need one MFA device to sign in to the AWS Management Console or create a session through the AWS CLI.

note: d098. Older questions assume one virtual MFA device per user. Passkeys as an MFA factor (What's New 2024-06-11 in the change feed) have no quotable dated page: see mine-changes.json. Current truth: iam-mfa-devices-up-to-eight.

claim: On 2025-01-30 AWS enhanced the IAM documentation of policy evaluation logic with improved flow charts and clearer explanations of how AWS decides to allow or deny a request.
question: What changed on the IAM policy evaluation logic page in January 2025?

evidence.quote: | [Updates to policy evaluation logic](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/IAM/latest/UserGuide/reference_policies_evaluation-logic.html) | Enhanced documentation for policy evaluation logic, including improved flow charts and clearer explanations of how AWS evaluates policies to determine whether to allow or deny a request. | January 30, 2025 |

When a user belongs to an account that is a member of an organization and accesses a resource that doesn't have a resource-based policy configured, the resulting permissions are the intersection of the user's policies, service control policies (SCPs), and resource control policy (RCP). This means that an action must be allowed by all three policy types.

note: d104. The history row describes a documentation update; the current page puts SCPs and RCPs in the flow. The evaluation rules themselves (explicit deny wins) are unchanged.
